Wiltshire man named Workplace Hero after saving life

25th November
Health
People
By Michael Ribbeck Reporter

Share

0 comments
Read More

'excellent' industry rating
Adrian (Ade) Cummings and Paul McGettigan (Image: Jonny Clarke)

A man who saved a life using first aid has been named a national Workplace Hero by St John Ambulance.

Adrian Cummins, 41, from Wiltshire, was honoured at the charity’s first-ever Lifesavers at Work Awards after he performed CPR on a man who collapsed in cardiac arrest outside his workplace.

The vehicle data manager works at Holman UK in Corsham.

M4 truck stop to expand again as lorry spaces fill up

Mr Cummins, known as Ade by friends and family, became a trained first aider shortly after the birth of his daughter, said the training kicked in immediately that day.

He recognised the man’s laboured, snoring-type breathing as agonal breathing, a key sign of cardiac arrest he’d learned during his training, and started CPR, continuing even after hearing the man’s ribs crack.

A colleague arrived with a defibrillator, and paramedics later told Mr Cummins that his actions had almost certainly saved the man’s life.

Paul McGettigan, the man he saved, said: “What Ade’s given me is more time.

"He’s given me time back with my family that I may have lost. I’m grateful I’ve got a second chance.”

The awards, held at The Museum of the Order of St John, recognised seven people across the UK whose quick thinking and first aid knowledge made a life-or-death difference.

Shona Dunn, chief executive of St John Ambulance, said: "Every one of the winners was an ordinary person who refused to give up on someone whose life was slipping away.

"These people are alive today because someone nearby knew what to do, and that should be true for everyone in this country."

St John Ambulance launched the awards in response to research showing that four in five UK workers believe lifesavers deserve more celebration than Oscar winners.

The charity now wants every employer in England to make first aid training part of working life.

Ms Dunn said: "Cardiac arrest is the emergency that workers fear the most, yet two in five say they wouldn’t know how to perform CPR.

"That’s a gap we can close, and the workplace is where we can close it the fastest."

'Strong objections' as councillors try to block new Greggs bakery

The awards also recognised first aiders who responded to emergencies outside the workplace, including three staff members from Windlesham House School who helped save the life of a cyclist who collapsed nearby.

Other honourees included companies such as TotalEnergies, which revamped its first aid programme following a workplace cardiac arrest, and Manchester Metropolitan University, which has trained nearly 3,000 students in first aid and mental health support.

The awards come amid findings that more than one in four UK workers have needed first aid at work, yet of those who have witnessed a medical emergency at work, just two in five (40%) were able to give first aid themselves.
